claims_disputed.claim: Generator-evaluatee bias is negligible on the primary metric.
claims_disputed.reason: The only evidence is DeepSeek 0.892 vs Claude 0.891 in code-only (Table 6). That parity cannot tell 'no bias' apart from 'Claude inflated by bias but otherwise weaker'. Testing it needs a second gold-answer generator or a generator swap, and the paper runs neither. The paper itself explains Claude's significant +0.026 documented delta (App. H Table 12) as 'generator advantage', which concedes a bias. Claude also leads closed-book on code-derivable tasks (0.560 vs 0.442-0.514), where reading code cannot help, which fits gold answers phrased the way Claude phrases them.

pattern_stance_changes.reason: The isolating comparison (same agent with repository access vs closed-book) is not split. It wins for all four models on both task sets: doc-dependent 0.629 to 0.860 with non-overlapping per-model CIs (App. H Table 11), and code-derivable 0.500 to 0.857, p<0.001. The doc-dependent set is the non-circular test, because its gold answers were written from documentation only, with no code tools (§4.5). Recomputing a 2-axis score without the saturated specificity axis from Table 7 still gives +0.234 vs +0.231, so the gain is not a scoring artifact. The review's caveats (no RAG or graph alternative, famous repositories, near-ceiling scores) limit strength and transfer, but they are not a split result. On private code the closed-book arm would do worse, not better.

Lexical retrieval is the agent's only retrieval in every condition: regex search_code over .py files plus list_directory and read_file (§4.3, §6.1). The paper uses the pattern throughout and compares it with no other retrieval design. That is 'introduces', not a mention.

A single GPT-5.4 rubric judge (§5.3, App. C) produces every number in the paper, and it has no inter-judge or human agreement check (§8 Limitations). The pattern is used centrally without an isolating comparison, which is 'introduces'.

missed_issues: The search tool only covers Python files: search_code is 'regex over all .py files' (§4.3), and the evaluation agent reuses the same tool definitions (§6.1). In the documented condition, README, .md and .rst docs can only be found by listing directories, even though the prompt tells the agent to start with them. Δdoc therefore measures mostly docstrings and comments plus whatever doc files the agent happens to open. The paper reports no turn, token or cost counts per condition, so the explanation for Gemini's -0.018 (turns spent on docs) is untested.

The 'generator advantage' explanation for Claude's +0.026 documented-minus-code-only delta on code-derivable tasks (Table 12) does not work. A generator advantage would lift Claude equally in both repository conditions, not create a gap between them. Gold answers were written by an agent exploring the repository with documentation present, starting from a doc chunk (§4.3), and only an LLM auditor removed doc-only claims. Residual doc leakage is an equally good explanation, and it weakens the 'code-derivable' label that the paper's validation rests on.

Table 8 pools 4 models x 132 tasks as 528 independent observations per cell. So the only significant category delta (Where +0.011, d=0.13, p=0.003 against α=0.0125) is pseudo-replicated and would likely not survive resampling clustered by task. The review's P39 note relies on it ('docs act as a navigation index').

The paper's check that the +0.23 headline survives without the specificity axis cites App. I, but App. I contains only per-repository code-only scores (Table 13). Recomputing from Table 7 confirms the check (mean gain +0.234 without specificity vs +0.231 with it), so claim 1 stays moderate, but the review's methodology entry repeats the wrong citation.

The significance language is looser than the numbers. The Table 6 caption says DeepSeek and Kimi have p>0.03, while App. H Table 12 gives 0.039 and 0.033 with 95% CIs spanning zero; p is a one-sided crossing proportion set against two-sided CIs. Gemini's p=0.004 is called 'marginally significant' although it fails the paper's own α=0.003.

There is no identifier-obfuscation ablation (§8). Code-only scores of 0.77-0.89 may rest on descriptive names plus memorized knowledge of famous libraries (closed-book 0.44-0.68). Treat them as an upper bound for private code with drifted or misleading names (compare 2609.26388).
note: I agree with the review's verdict, its COI call and its scores within one point; I give reproducibility 3 because prompts are in App. C and E-G, commits are pinned and the bootstrap seed is stated. I agree that the documentation-utility and validation claims are weak, for the reasons the review gives: doc-derived gold answers, a doc-first prompt in the documented arm, and a self-confirming filter. The search tool's .py-only scope weakens the documentation claim further. I lower 'generator bias is negligible' to unsupported, because one score tie cannot test it and the paper's own reading of Claude's +0.026 admits a bias. I upgrade P43 from mixed to supports, because the code-access comparison wins everywhere, including on gold answers written only from docs and under a recomputed score without specificity; the missing RAG or graph baseline limits what it supports, not its direction. P05 and P18 are used throughout without alternatives, so they are 'introduces', not 'neutral'.
